$doc: Rendering + lighting. There is no player flashlight - every room lights itself, and `minAmbientFloor` is the hard 'dark but never blind' guarantee. Maps override these via config/maps.json. Light values are real three.js units (ambient/point intensity, candela for points) - the renderer applies no hidden scaling.
$fullscreen: Whether the game starts fullscreen. The player's own switch is `options.fullscreen` in the save profile; a browser can only act on it after a gesture, so it is restored at boot in the packaged build alone.
$powerPreference: Which GPU to ask for, on a machine with more than one. A laptop with an Intel chip and a discrete card gives WebGL the INTEGRATED one unless a page asks otherwise, and it is not close - that is the difference between a machine that runs this and one that does not, and it is the machines this setting exists for that have two GPUs. `high-performance` asks for the discrete one; `low-power` is the browser default and would trade the frame rate for battery. Like `antialias`, it is a context attribute fixed when the context is created, so no quality tier may change it.
$brightness: The options-menu brightness slider MULTIPLIES `exposure` rather than replacing it, so a map that deliberately darkens itself stays relatively darker at every setting. 1.0 is exactly what the map asked for.
$lights: three.js compiles a shader program per material PER LIGHT COUNT, so a light set that changes size mid-run recompiles the whole map a room at a time - which is a frozen frame every time. `maxActiveLights` and `shadows.maxCastingLights` are therefore a fixed BUDGET, not a cap: the renderer always enables exactly this many of each (nearest first), so the count a shader sees never changes once a world is up. A lamp enabled out of range costs a slot and contributes nothing, which is the point.
$lightFadeSeconds: A lamp taking or losing one of those slots fades rather than switches, or you watch rooms come on as you walk up to them. The handover is sequential - the outgoing lamp goes to black, then the slot changes hands, then the new one comes up - so this is half of a full changeover.

shadows.$maxCastingLights: Of `maxActiveLights`, how many are always shadow casters. Room lamps declare their own `castShadow` (at most one per room, see art/ROOM_FORMAT.md) and their maps are baked once at load, so this is a fragment-shader cost, not a per-frame render.

$quality: Player-facing quality tiers. Each is an OVERLAY merged over everything above, exactly the way a map's or a difficulty's overrides are, so a tier is data and adding one is a config change. `default` is what a profile that has never opened the options menu plays on. Only put things in here that are worth a frame on a slow machine AND cost little to look at: the four below are, in measured order of what they buy, the pixel count, the shadow casters, the light budget and the render distance. `antialias` is deliberately absent - it is a WebGL context flag, so changing it needs the context rebuilt, and a setting that quietly waits for a restart is worse than one that is not offered.
$note: `maxActiveLights` and `shadows.maxCastingLights` take effect on the NEXT scene, not immediately: the whole point of a fixed light budget is that a shader's light count never changes while a world is up (see `$lights`). Everything else here applies the moment it is chosen.

quality.$probe: On the FIRST launch on a machine and never again, the game measures itself and picks a starting tier - silently, before the menu is drawn. It draws `drawCalls` separately-drawn boxes lit by `maxActiveLights` lights at the window's size, which is the shape a real frame turned out to have, and times a block of `frames` of them. `default` above is what a machine that beats every threshold gets. See src/render/probe.ts for why this is a benchmark rather than a table of GPU names.
quality.$thresholds: Tried in order, first match wins, so the slowest tier is listed FIRST - and every unknown (a probe that threw, a context that would not open, a warm-up over `budgetMs`) resolves to that first entry, so it must stay the slowest one. `atLeastMs` is the probed frame time at or above which a machine gets that tier. Derived from a 60 fps target rather than by feel: the reference machine probes at 0.8-1.7 ms and draws the heaviest map at 3.6 ms, so a real frame costs roughly 3-4.5x a probed one. Taking the pessimistic end of that, 16.7 ms of real frame is about 3.7 ms of probe - hence 3.5 for `medium`. Past about 6 ms even the low tier cannot hold 60 fps on Kerberos Deep, so from there the machine should have every saving going. The reference machine sits 2x under the nearest threshold, which is the margin that stops run-to-run noise deciding anything.

low.$shadows: Zero CASTERS rather than `enabled: false`, so this and the player's own shadow switch never contradict each other. With no lamp in the casting pool no shadow map is ever rendered, which is the same saving; turning the switch itself off from here would leave it reading `on` in a menu while doing nothing.

culling.$doc: The manor is a graph of sealed boxes joined by doorways, so 'can this room be seen' has an exact answer: flood out from the cell the camera stands in, through openings that are not shut doors, narrowing the screen rectangle at every doorway. A room nothing can see into is not drawn. This runs INSIDE `renderDistanceRooms` - it can only ever hide something the distance test was already about to hide, so it cannot introduce pop-in.
culling.$margins: Safety. `portalMarginMetres` widens each doorway before it is projected, because the wall reveal around an opening is visible at grazing angles - that one is worth having. `screenMargin` widens the projected rectangle, in fractions of half the viewport, and is only numerical slack: the camera is set in the same simulation tick that culls, and does not move between the frames drawn from it, so there is no lag to cover. It compounds through every doorway in a sight line, so keep it small - 0.1 cost a third of the draw calls in an opened-up map.

lobby.$doc: Overrides merged over the block above while the lobby scene is up. The lobby is the one bright place in the game: daylight off snow, a fire, and only enough fog to give the mountains depth.
lobby.$maxActiveLights: One number above what the cabin actually builds (sun, snow bounce, warm fill, chandelier, poster wash, fire, the lamp inside the mirror, the one over the dartboard), so the nearest-N ranking never has to choose and the sun can never be the light that loses. A map has thirty-odd rooms to ration lights between; the lobby is one hand-built space with nothing else in the scene.
lobby.$note: Fog is thin enough to leave the cabin crisp and thick enough to give the mountains aerial perspective - at 130 m it is already half fog colour.
